_comment: THE BOUNDARY RULE, AS DATA, BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN TWICE AND NOTHING COMPARED THE COPIES.
Two suites assert who may know about the identifier-encoding seam, deliberately, because
they run in different recipes: `tests/tidentifierencoding.nim` is in `just test`, which
takes about 37 minutes, and `tools/chain/identifier-encoding-selftest.mjs` is in
`just chain-selftest`, the fast gate people actually run. A boundary that only the slow
gate knew about would be a boundary nobody saw move.
── WHY THE RULE IS HERE AND NOT IN EITHER OF THEM ────────────────────────────────────
Because it was in BOTH of them. The source extensions, the pruned directory names, the
per-directory population floors and the allowlists were spelled out twice and compared to
nothing, and the two halves agreed only because two independently-maintained copies
happened to match. That is not a property, it is a coincidence with a maintenance cost,
and it had already broken once: the Nim half pruned `dist/` with an unanchored
`contains("dist/")` while the JavaScript half pruned by exact directory NAME, so a single
`client/src/redist/x.mjs` put the two populations at 102 and 103. That was found by hand
and fixed by hand, which is exactly the failure mode a single source removes.
So the rule is one file that both halves read, for the reason `identifier-encodings.json`,
`refusal-reasons.json` and `snapshot-format.json` beside it are data: a rule that has to
hold in two languages cannot live in one of them.
── AND THE RULE BEING SHARED IS NOT ENOUGH, WHICH IS THE SECOND HALF ─────────────────
The `redist/` divergence was NOT a disagreement about the rule. Both halves already agreed
that `dist/` is pruned; they disagreed about what `dist/` MEANS, in their own sweep code,
in two languages. Moving the words here would not have caught it.
So the Nim half additionally runs the JavaScript half with `--emit-population` and requires
the two swept file LISTS to be identical, per top-level directory, as sets. That is a check
on the two IMPLEMENTATIONS rather than on the two configurations, and it is the one that
bites on a prune, a glob or a git-population rule that two languages read differently.
Each sweep names the TOKENS whose appearance in a source file makes that file a consumer
of one half of the seam, and enumerates exactly which files may name them. The comparison
is an EQUALITY against a sweep of the whole tree, not a subset check: an unexpected
consumer fails it in one direction and an expected consumer that stopped being one fails
it in the other. The `count` beside each expected list is asserted too, so the list cannot
drift upward one entry at a time with the equality quietly edited to match — a number is a
thing a reviewer sees move.
declaration  who reads `chains[<slug>].identifierEncoding`, the registry member that
says how a chain writes its identifiers. NAMING ALONE WAS MEASURED
LEAKING, which is why the equality is against a sweep: consumers planted
one file over from two named files (`client/src/viewmodel/chain_vm.nim`
beside `chain_registry_vm.nim`, `tools/capture/lib/provenance.mjs` beside
`entities.mjs`) once left every arm green while a universal claim printed.
caseRule     who reads the PER-ENCODING CASE RULE — `identifierKeyForm`,
`identifierDisplayForm`, `identifierPayload`. These are a separate sweep
rather than more tokens on the first one because they are a separate
fact: a file may key an identifier without ever reading a registry row
(the §5 hash index does, under a named global encoding), and a file may
read the row without keying anything (the session pins it). Folding them
together would let one seam's new consumer be excused by the other's
allowlist.
A sweep that found nothing would satisfy every equality above perfectly, because an empty
set equals an empty set. So each top-level directory carries a FLOOR on the number of
source files swept, per directory, so an emptied sweep of one cannot hide behind another.
The floors are the contract; the COUNT is an observation each run prints. Both halves take
their population from git — tracked plus untracked-and-not-ignored — so it moves with the
working tree, and a number pinned here would go stale for anyone holding a scratch file.
(The Justfile header once pinned one and was stale within a day.)
`.gitignore` is where 'this is generated' is already written down, and it is kept current
by whoever adds the recipe. A same-stem heuristic — a `.js` beside a `.nim` of the same
name is `nim js` output — was tried, was measured against the one case it hit
(`client/tests/test_searchboot.js`), and walked straight past `client/Justfile`'s
`search-bundle`, which compiles `searchboot/searchboot.nim` to `searchboot/search.js`:
different stem, so `search.js` was swept as source and reddened the client equality for
anyone who had ever built the bundle, while a clean checkout and CI never saw it. A gate
green where it is checked and red where it is used is worse than one that is merely wrong.
Tracked PLUS untracked-and-not-ignored is the population: the second half is what catches
a consumer that has been written and not yet committed, which is when catching it is most
useful. `ci/test/client-sdk-boundary.sh` derives its population the same way.
A boundary check that only watched the CLOSED half of the seam would report the seam shut.
`pins` states what is still hex-shaped and what must no longer be there, as counts over
CODE rather than over comments — counted over comments, a paragraph explaining a defect
reads as the defect. Each pin is expected to go red in its turn, at which point whoever
moved it reads the reason recorded beside it.

sweeps.why: who reads the registry member that says how a chain writes its identifiers

src.why: builds, validates and reads it, over the closed set
the ONE derivation, which takes the token as a parameter
the path builders, which name the kind each segment comes from
the SDK facade's own documentation of that signature
pins the chain's declaration like the generation
hands the session's declaration to the paths
reads the declaration out of the tree it is validating

client.why: the browser's search bootstrap, which recomputes the producer's path in a tab

tools.why: the JavaScript half's selftest, and still nothing else: the capture tooling enumerates what was published rather than deriving it

sweeps.why: who reads the per-encoding CASE rule — the step that replaced one global toLowerAscii

src.why: reads the `case` rule out of the shared file and answers over it
folds per encoding before it slices, so a shard key is recomputable from either spelling
the §5 index's shard key and its hex-pair parser, under the named global `HashIndexEncoding`
the object-name segment of every sharded path is the identifier's key form
the SDK read answers with the DISPLAY form the tree states rather than echoing the caller's spelling back
checks that a published tree states the key form in its paths and the display form in its bodies

client.why: canonicalises a hex query to the form the published index and object names are keyed by

present.why: THE INDEX STILL PARSES HEX PAIRS, so a base58 or bech32 identifier has no representation in it at all. Published self-describing wire format: widening it is a migration of every published shard plus a compatibility window (Publishing-And-Caching.md §6.1, §6.2) and lands alone.

…and that assumption is NAMED rather than anonymous. §5's index path carries no chain segment, so a client resolving a bare query cannot know which chain's declaration to normalise with: this index's key rule has to be global. One greppable constant is what the migration will widen.

THE ONE REMAINING FOLD IN THIS MODULE, COUNTED RATHER THAN FORBIDDEN, because it is not a normalisation of anybody's identifier: `bytesToHex` renders STORED BYTES back into the index's key encoding, and lowercase hex IS that encoding rather than a decision about case. The fold that WAS a decision — `stripHex`, applied to every identifier of every encoding — is on the absent list below. Counting this one is what stops a second appearing beside it.

absent.why: GONE, not kept as a wrapper. It folded case unconditionally for every encoding — right for hex, destroys base58 and base64url — and a correctly-named hex-assuming entry point one identifier away from every call site is reachable by habit and indistinguishable from a choice in a diff.

present.why: the two literal `0x` filters over published directory ENTRIES. These enumerate the tree the hash index keys, so they genuinely follow the index: a filter widened ahead of the index would enumerate a non-hex chain's entities and then fail to key them, which is worse than not seeing them.

the three former derivation sites, now enumerations. THE COUNT IS THE PIN: a fourth sharded path in this file either adds a fourth call here — which moves this number — or open-codes a slice, which the `absent` list below refuses. Before this, both halves counted only the `0x` filters, so a fourth `slice(2, 6)` was invisible to both.

absent.why: the open-coded hex shard rule, at three sites, building `/d/{chain}/tx/{shard}/`, `/d/{chain}/ts/{tsv}/{shard}/` and `/d/{chain}/g/{gen}/addr/{shard}/`. It DERIVED rather than enumerated, so the 'it follows the index' defence never covered it; it was also stricter than the function it duplicated, with neither the strip-only-if-present quirk nor the right-padding.
the tooling reads what was published rather than the declaration behind it, which is why it needs no JavaScript reader of the closed set.
